items.prompt: Why are night-blooming flowers usually white?

options.label: White shows up best in dim light
options.feedback: It reflects whatever faint light there is.

options.label: White petals last longer
options.feedback: Colour has no effect on how long a petal survives.

options.label: Night pollinators avoid colour
options.feedback: Moths see colour, and some see it very well.

options.label: Pigments break down in the dark
options.feedback: Pigments are stable whether lit or not.

items.ok_line: The brightest thing available, against a dark background.
items.ko_line: Ask which colour stands out when there is almost nothing to see by.
items.exp_title: Built to be found by moonlight
items.exp_text: A flower open at night must be found by a moth in near-darkness, and white reflects more of the little light available than any other colour. Under moonlight a white petal is unmistakable while a red one reads as black — the eye's dim-light cells barely register red at all. The same flowers are usually large and pale-edged, which makes them stand out further still.

items.prompt: Why do night flowers give off such a strong scent?

options.label: Scent carries where colour cannot
options.feedback: A moth finds the flower by smell before it sees it.

options.label: Cool air destroys scent faster
options.feedback: Cool still air holds scent better than warm air.

options.label: It keeps insects from eating them
options.feedback: The scent attracts rather than repels.

options.label: Scent replaces the need for nectar
options.feedback: The nectar is still the reward on offer.

items.ok_line: In the dark, advertising has to be done by smell.
items.ko_line: The flower cannot be seen from far off. So how does anything find it?
items.exp_text: A daytime flower can signal with colour from metres away; a night flower cannot, so it invests in scent instead. Many release their perfume only after dark, on a schedule set by an internal clock, and stop by morning — there is no point paying for a signal nobody is answering. Still night air disperses scent slowly, so a plume can hold together and lead a moth in from a considerable distance.

items.prompt: Which insect pollinates most night-opening flowers?

options.label: The moth
options.feedback: Long-tongued hawkmoths especially, hovering as they feed.

options.label: The honeybee
options.feedback: Bees return to the hive at dusk and stay there.

options.label: The butterfly
options.feedback: Butterflies fly by day and roost at night.

options.label: The ladybird
options.feedback: Ladybirds eat aphids and visit few flowers.

items.ok_line: Moths do the night shift, and the flowers are shaped for them.
items.ko_line: The pollinator has to be flying after dark. That rules out most of them.
items.exp_text: Hawkmoths are the main visitors: strong fliers that hover in front of a flower and feed through a long coiled tongue, so night flowers tend to be pale, deeply tubular and heavily scented. Bats do the same work in the tropics for larger blooms. In some places the two systems are so distinct that a plant family will have day-flowering species pollinated by bees and night-flowering relatives shaped entirely for moths.

items.prompt: What did Darwin predict from the shape of a Madagascan orchid?

options.label: A moth with an enormous tongue
options.feedback: One was found four decades later, as described.

options.label: That the flower had no pollinator
options.feedback: He argued the opposite from its shape.

options.label: That it pollinated itself
options.feedback: The long tube would make no sense if it did.

options.label: That birds must be feeding on it
options.feedback: No bird could reach down such a tube.

items.ok_line: He described the animal before anyone had seen it.
items.ko_line: The nectar sat at the bottom of a tube 30 cm long. Something had to be reaching it.
items.exp_title: A prediction that took forty years
items.exp_text: In 1862 Darwin examined an orchid whose nectar lay at the base of a tube nearly 30 cm long and concluded that a moth with a tongue of matching length must exist in Madagascar. He was widely mocked. Such a moth was described in 1903, twenty-one years after his death, and was named praedicta. It was not filmed feeding at the flower until 1992.

items.prompt: How does a flower know when to open?

options.label: An internal clock, corrected by light
options.feedback: It keeps opening on time even in constant darkness.

options.label: It opens when the temperature drops
options.feedback: Temperature adjusts the timing, but does not set it.

options.label: It opens when an insect lands
options.feedback: The flower opens before any visitor arrives.

options.label: It opens when the air becomes damp
options.feedback: Humidity is not the trigger.

items.ok_line: A clock inside the plant, reset each day by the light.
items.ko_line: Kept in permanent darkness, the flower still opens near the right hour. What does that mean?
items.exp_text: Plants carry a circadian clock built from proteins that accumulate and break down over roughly twenty-four hours. Kept in constant darkness, flowers go on opening and closing near their usual times for days, drifting slowly — proof the rhythm is internal and daylight only resets it. Linnaeus proposed a flower clock in 1751, a bed planted so that the hour could be read from which species was open.

items.prompt: What is unusual about the flowering of the night-blooming cereus?

options.label: It opens for a single night
options.feedback: By sunrise the flower has withered for good.

options.label: It flowers every night for a month
options.feedback: It flowers once, briefly, and rarely.

options.label: It opens only in bright moonlight
options.feedback: Moon phase does not control it.

options.label: It flowers underground
options.feedback: The bloom is held well clear of the ground.

items.ok_line: One night, and by morning it is finished.
items.ko_line: People sit up all night to watch it. That should tell you how long it lasts.
items.exp_text: The night-blooming cereus opens after dark for a single night, sometimes only once in a year, and is spent by sunrise. Plants in an area often bloom on the same night, which concentrates the moths and makes cross-pollination far likelier. Botanical gardens announce the event and stay open late for it. The flower can be over 20 cm across and its scent carries a remarkable distance.

items.prompt: Why do some tropical flowers open at night for bats?

options.label: Bats carry pollen much further
options.feedback: They travel far more each night than an insect.

options.label: Bats eat the insects that compete
options.feedback: Nectar bats do not hunt insects.

options.label: Bats can see the flowers in colour
options.feedback: Nectar bats mostly find flowers by smell and echo.

options.label: Bats damage the flower less
options.feedback: A bat is far rougher than a moth.

items.ok_line: A bat can carry pollen across a valley in one night.
items.ko_line: Think about how far a bat travels in a night compared with a moth.
items.exp_text: A nectar bat may cover tens of kilometres in a night, far more than any insect, which matters for trees scattered thinly through a forest. Bat-pollinated flowers are correspondingly built: large, sturdy, dull-coloured, opening downward and clear of the foliage, with a musty scent and copious nectar. Some carry curved petals that act as an acoustic mirror, bouncing a bat's echolocation call straight back to advertise their position.

items.prompt: Why do many flowers close their petals at night?

options.label: To protect the pollen from damp
options.feedback: Dew and cold would spoil it before morning.

options.label: To rest after a day of work
options.feedback: A flower does no work that needs rest.

options.label: To trap insects until morning
options.feedback: A few do, but almost none for that reason.

options.label: To stop growing overnight
options.feedback: Closing does not halt growth.

items.ok_line: Pollen is the investment, and dew would ruin it.
items.ko_line: Ask what the flower has inside that would suffer from a night of cold and wet.
items.exp_text: Closing at night keeps dew and cold off the pollen and the reproductive parts, and the pollinators those flowers depend on are asleep anyway, so nothing is lost. Some close in rain as well. Tulips do it by growing one side of the petal faster than the other according to temperature, so a tulip in a warm room opens and cannot shut again.

items.prompt: How does a moth locate a flower from far away in the dark?

options.label: It flies upwind along a scent plume
options.feedback: Losing the trail, it casts sideways until it finds it again.

options.label: It sees the flower's pale glow
options.feedback: Sight only helps in the last few metres.

options.label: It hears the flower opening
options.feedback: A flower opens silently.

options.label: It returns to a remembered place
options.feedback: Memory helps, but it finds new flowers too.

items.ok_line: Upwind, casting sideways whenever the trail is lost.
items.ko_line: The signal is a scent carried on the air. How would you follow one?
items.exp_text: Scent does not spread as a smooth cone but as a ragged plume of filaments. A moth flies upwind while it detects the scent and, on losing it, turns and casts across the wind until it picks the plume up again — producing the zig-zag flight path that leads it to the source. Only in the final metres does vision take over, guiding it onto the pale petals.

items.prompt: Why does a moonflower open in a matter of minutes?

options.label: Water is pumped into the petal cells
options.feedback: They stiffen and unfurl as they fill.

options.label: The petals dry out and spring apart
options.feedback: Drying makes a petal shrivel, not open.

options.label: The wind pulls them open
options.feedback: It opens on perfectly still nights.

options.label: The stem lengthens and pulls them
options.feedback: The stem plays no part in unfurling.

items.ok_line: Water pressure, and the petal unwinds like a spring.
items.ko_line: A plant has no muscles. What else could push a petal outward?
items.exp_text: Plants move by controlling water. Cells on one side of the petal take in water and swell, and the petal unrolls — a moonflower can go from bud to fully open in two or three minutes, fast enough to watch. The same mechanism closes a Venus flytrap and folds a mimosa leaf when touched. No plant has muscle; every movement it makes is water going somewhere.
